title: Tell the beloved friend
hookLine: the Tenth Guru's song in the wilderness after Chamkaur: tell the beloved friend the state of his disciples (Dasam, Khayal Patshahi 10)

lines: ALONE IN THE FOREST, HE SINGS.
cards: A mud fortress at Chamkaur in Punjab, surrounded by a much larger army. Inside, Guru Gobind Singh and a small band of Sikhs.
By the end of the fighting, his two elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, have fallen, along with many of his companions. At the Sikhs' insistence, the Guru leaves in the dark.
Sikh tradition remembers him alone in the forest near Machhiwara, on the cold ground, his clothes torn. And there, it says, he sang.

teach.b: The song is called a khayal, and it's in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings associated with the Tenth Guru. Much of that collection is in Braj, an old literary language of north India.
This song is in Punjabi, simple and close. It begins: mitra piaare noo, haal mureedaan daa kahinaa.
In paraphrase: go, tell the beloved Friend the state of His disciples.
Without You, soft quilts are like sickness, and living in comfortable houses is like living with snakes. The water jug is like a spike, the cup like a dagger.
And then: a straw mat with the Friend is better than grand houses that burn like a furnace. The Friend is God. A disciple, a mureed, sends word to the Beloved by any messenger who'll go.
What's striking is what's not in it. No complaint about the enemy, no counting of losses, no call for revenge.
A father who has just lost two sons speaks only of being apart from God, and of preferring the hardest ground with God to every comfort without Him.
Historians debate when the khayal was written, and the tradition that places it at Machhiwara is just that, a tradition. But for Sikhs, that setting is how the song is heard.
It's often sung slowly and softly: a tender song from a Guru whose life was full of steel.
It's sent, as a message, to the Friend.

how: Sikhs sing mitra piaare noo softly in kirtan, and it is often sung in December, during the weeks that recall Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the Guru's sons.

o: a loyal disciple of the Guru

games.q: the song in the forest — tap the pairs.

games.q: you've lost your sons and your companions, and you're alone on the cold ground. what does the song send to the Friend?
o: a list of what was lost.
word of the disciples' state: without You, every comfort is sickness.
a plan for the next battle.
games.why: the song asks only to tell the Friend: the straw bed with Him is dearer than every comfort without Him.

practice: Think of someone you haven't told how things really are with you, and picture what you'd say, plainly, without dressing it up.
If you pray, tell God the same thing in your own words first, or say Waheguru and let that be the message.

wordCard.voice: Mitra piaare, beloved friend: Guru Gobind Singh's khayal, remembered as sung in the forest after Chamkaur, tells Him His disciples' state; the Friend's straw bed is better than any palace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: beloved friend; the khayal's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: tell the friend. Grief doesn't have to be hidden; it can be sent. Until tomorrow.
